Introduction
Cattle fertility is a crucial aspect that should be considered in breeding operations. Ovarian inactivity is a major 
contributing factor to reduced fertility in farm animals in 
most of developing countries with significant economic 
losses due to low calf production and milk yield [1]. 
Numerous factors have been reported to affect the occurrence of ovarian inactivity such as the geographic environment, breed, species, season, level of nutrition and 
hormones [2]. Improvement in cattle has been focused on 
productive and reproductive traits. Some fertility indices 
like age at first calving (AFC) and calving interval (CI) are

Abstract
Background There are no studies belong NOTCH2 gene polymorphism in relation to reproductive and 
productive traits in Holstein cattle. The objective of the present study was to investigate the effect of NOTCH2 gene 
polymorphisms on productive and reproductive performance of fertile and anestrum cattle.
Methods The cattle were classified into anestrus for 3–12 months postpartum (n=115, 37.7%) and normal cyclic 
fertile (n=190, 62.3%). Age at 1st calving, calving interval, calf birth weight, milk yield and days of milking data were 
obtained from the farm records for all animals. Blood samples were collected from fertile and anestrum animals for 
DNA extraction and the PCR as well as single-strand conformation polymorphism techniques (SSCP) were performed 
for detection of the NOTCH2 gene polymorphism.
Results The sequencing results showed that NOTCH2 gene in cattle is polymorphic with 5 genotypes AA, AG, GG, 
CC and CT. Four novel SNPs as transition single base substitution mutations were detected at 3: 23,192,033 (A/G), 
3:23192149 (C/T), 3:23192071 (C/T) and 3:23192143 (G/A). GG genotype of NOTCH2 gene was associated with shorter 
calving interval and heavier calf birth weight in both fertile and anestrum cattle.
Conclusions NOTCH2 gene in cattle could be used as a genetic marker involved in reproductive traits in both fertile 
and anestrum cattle.
Keywords NOTCH2 gene, Polymorphism, SNPs, Fertility, Productive traits
Four SNPs in the untranslated region of the 
NOTCH2 gene involved in reproductive traits 
in fertile and anestrum Holstein Friesian cattle

obtained by recording organizations [3]. However, data 
recording takes a long time. AFC is thought to be a significant predictor of future milk yield in Holstein Friesian 
(HF) dairy cattle [4]. CI has traditionally been the main 
indicator of reproduction in animals during their productive lives, especially in dairy cattle [5]. There seems to be 
a strong negative correlation between the AFC and the 
CI. The characterization of the chromosomal areas that 
regulate CI and AFC in cattle contributes to the genetic 
improvement by recognizing candidate genes that help in 
understanding their reproductive physiology [6].
The birth weight (BW) of a calf is the first trait being 
measured and is a highly useful economic indicator in the 
beef cattle industry [7]. The genetic link between BW and 
reproductive traits such as AFC and gestation Length 
(GL) indicated that choosing a calf with a higher BW 
could lead to longer GL and AFC [8].
The Notch signaling system is essential for cell-to-cell 
communication, proliferation, controlling cell fate determination, and death throughout tissue morphogenesis, 
as well as homeostasis and regeneration [9]. Bonadeo et 
al. [10] studied the Notch system’s role in the development of the mammary gland of Holstein heifers and cited 
that NOTCH2 active domains increased during pubertal 
phases through Notch receptor expression and localization in the mammary gland in pre- and post-pubertal 
stages. Several genes of Notch signaling pathway are 
expressed in mammalian ovaries, including four Notch

receptors (Notch1- Notch4) and six Notch ligands (Jagged1, Jagged2, Hes1, Hes5, Hey1, Hey2) all of which imply 
that this signaling pathway is involved in follicular development [11, 12]. NOTCH2 receptor is a crucial member 
of Notch signaling and expressed at high levels in theca 
and granulosa cells of ovarian follicles [13]. It has been 
revealed that the growth of granulosa cells is dependent on Notch signaling [14]. The knockout of NOTCH2
reduces cell proliferation and increases apoptosis in 
mouse follicular granulosa cells explaining the aberrant 
follicles [15]. There are no data about NOTCH gene polymorphism and ovarian activity in bovine as well as age 
at 1st calving and calving interval. However, it remains 
unknown about the specific role of the NOTCH pathway 
and fertility in bovine. We suggest that the NOTCH signaling pathway is essential for controlling the productive 
and reproductive performance of fertile and anestrum 
cattle. Therefore, our study aimed at clarifying the association between NOTCH 2 polymorphism with age at 1st 
calving, calving interval, calf birth weight, milk yield and 
days of milking in fertile and anestrum cows.
Materials and methods
Animal and samples
This study was carried out on 305 Holstein Friesian (HF) 
cows at farm belongs to the Animal Production Research 
Institute located in Kafr El-Sheikh Governorate. The 
multiparous cows aged from 6 to 10 years were raised 
under consistent conditions of weather and nutrition. 
The cows were kept in barns, fed ad lib grass and water, 
and given around 3 kg of commercial concentrate per day 
for each cow. The animals were classified into anestrum 
for 3–12 months postpartum (n=115, 37.7%) and normal 
cyclic fertile (n=190, 62.3%). Age at 1st calving, calving 
interval, calf birth weight, milk yield and days of milking

data for the animals under the study were obtained from 
the farm records. The data for each animal were an average over multiple previous pregnancies. Rectal and ultrasonographic examination using a B-mode scanner were 
performed for each animal twice in four weeks period to 
determine the animal’s ovarian status. The corpus luteum 
and follicles bigger than 1  mm served as indicators of 
ovarian activity. Blood samples were collected from jugular veins of all the animals in vacutainer tubes containing 
EDTA at winter season, the temperature is not more than 
25 °C. The samples were kept at -20 C until used for DNA 
extraction.
DNA extraction and PCR amplification
Genomic DNA was extracted from blood samples using 
Blood DNA Preparation - Column Kit (Jena Bioscience, 
Jena, Germany) following the manufacturer’s instructions. DNA quality and quantity were measured using a 
Nano-Drop 1000 spectrophotometer (Thermo Scientific, 
Wilmington DE, USA). The samples had DNA concentrations between 1013 and 942 (ng/µl), adequate DNA 
purity and integrity, and an OD 260/280 of 1.85. The 
PCR amplification was performed using Bio-Rad thermal cycler (T 100, USA) using one set of primers (F: 5′
- CCTTTTAATCCCTGCTTCCACA −3′ and R: 5′ - A
TTGGGGAGAGGTACAATGCTG −3′) to amplify a 
partial upstream untranslated region of Notch 2 gene. 
Primer3 software version 4.0 (https://primer3.ut.ee/) was 
used to design the primers. The amplification reactions 
were prepared in volume of 50 µl containing 5.00 µl buffer 10x, 1.00 µl 2.5 mM (dNTPs mixture), 0.25 µl primer, 
0.30 µl Taq polymerase (5U/µl), 3.00 µl 25 mM (MgCL2),

35.20 µl water (nuclease free water) and 5.00 µl of DNA. 
The PCR conditions were; one cycle at 95 °C for 4 min. 
and 32 cycles at 94 °C for 30 s., 60 °C for 30 s. and 72 °C 
for 30  s then final extension of 72  °C for 5  min. Upon 
completion of the reaction, the products were exposed to 
electrophoresis in 1.7% agarose gel.
Single strand conformation polymorphism technique 
(SSCP)
SSCP was conducted on PCR product (216 bp) of Notch2 
gene to investigate the genetic variations in that fragment. PCR-SSCP technique was performed according to [16] and [17]. Briefly, the PCR products of 7.00 µl 
Mahmoud et al. BMC Veterinary Research (2024) 20:581 Page 3 of 8
had been mixed with 43  µl of denaturing solution, 
which composed of 98% formamide; 20mM EDTA, pH 
8.0; 0.05% xylene cyanol; 0.05%bromophenol blue and 
28 µl ddH2O. The denaturation was performed at 95 °C 
for 12  min. then cooling for 10  min on ice. The denatured samples were loaded onto 12% polyacrylamide 
gel containing (29:1 acrylamide: bis-acrylamide, 10  ml 
1xTBE buffer (Tris-base, Boric acid and EDTA), 2.5  ml 
glycerol, 17.5  ml deionized water, 400  µl APS solution 
(ammonium per sulfate) and 40  µl of TEMED (N, N, 
N´, N´-Tetramethyl ethylene diamine). Electrophoresis was done at 0.7 x TBE buffer 4 °C, 150 V, 60 mA for

15 h. Ethidium bromide (0.5 µg/ml) staining was used to 
visualize the isolated DNA-fragments on polyacrylamide 
gels and then photographed by Bio-Rad Gel-Doc System, 
USA.
Sequencing analysis
PCR purification spin procedure (QIAGEN) and QIAquick PCR purification kit (QIAGEN), which are 
intended for the isolation of DNA fragments from PCR 
reactions, were used to purify the PCR product. The samples were prepared for sequencing using an ABI PRISM 
3730XL analyzer (Macrogen, Seoul, South Korea), a 
Sanger sequencing instrument. BLAST program [18] 
was utilized for sequence identification and confirmation during the sequencing analysis and alignments. For 
sequence assembly, alignment, and SNP detection, the 
software programs Bioedit 7.0.5.3 [19] and CodonCode 
Aligner 10.0.2 (CodonCode Corp., Dedham, MA, USA) 
were utilized.
Statistical analysis
Data were analyzed by a two-way analysis of variance 
using the xlstat software and general linear model [20].
The main factors were animal status and genotype. The 
traits that were analyzed were age at 1st calving, calving 
interval, calf birth weight, milk yield and days of milking.
The following model was employed:
Yijk = µ + Li + Sj + LSij + eijk
Where:
Yijk: The kth observation of the jth genotype inside the 
ith animal status.
µ: Overall mean.
Li: Effect of the ith animal status (random effect).
Sj: Effect of the jth genotype (fixed effect).
LSij: Interaction between the ith animal status and the 
jth genotype.
Eijk: The random error.
The least square means (LSM)±standard errors (SE) 
are used to report all data. When significance was found, 
mean values were separated using Duncan’s multiple 
range test [21]. The 5% significance level was chosen.
Results
The PCR-SSCP technique was performed on the genomic

DNA of 301 HF cows to study the polymorphism in partial upstream-untranslated region of Notch 2 gene. The 
PCR amplified the targeted 216  bp fragments of Notch 
2 gene (Fig. 1). The PCR-SSCP analysis revealed 5 different patterns (Fig. 2). The sequence analysis of the different five patterns confirmed our results and the sequence 
Fig. 1 Ethidium bromide-stained gel of PCR amplification for NOTCH 2 gene. M: 100 & 50-bp ladder marker, -ve: control negative and 1–9: PCR product 
of 216-bp
Mahmoud et al. BMC Veterinary Research (2024) 20:581 Page 4 of 8
of the amplicon showed 5 different genotypes (AA, AG, 
GG, CC and CT) with 4 SNPs (Figs. 3 and 4) as transition single base substitution mutations located at 3: 
23,192,033 (A/G), 3:23192071 (C/T), 3:23192143 (G/A) 
and 3:23192149 (C/T). The identification numbers of 
SNPs were rs135569126, rs136361500, rs134288872 and 
rs136778944, respectively (Table  1). The AG genotype 
contained two mutations: a transformation from A to G 
(A/G) and from C to T (C/T). The CT genotype had four 
mutations: transformations from A to G, C to T, G to A, 
and C to T (A/G, C/T, G/A & C/T). Finally, the GG genotype had two mutations: C to T and A to G (C/T & A/G).
There is no significant difference in the frequencies 
of the genotypes and alleles of NOTCH 2 gene in both 
fertile and anestrum animals (Table  2). Holstein Friesian cattle populations under study were found to be in 
Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium using a chi square test. 
There are no significant differences in AFC, CI and calf 
birth weight between fertile and anestrum cows. While 
there are significantly, lower in milk yield of lactation and

days of milking in anestrum animals than fertile (Table 3). 
The GG genotype was connected to the shortest calving 
interval and the highest calf birth weight, while the CT 
genotype was linked to the highest average age at first 
calving.
There is interaction between the animal status and 
genotype (Table 3). The AFC significantly increased with 
CT genotype in fertile HF cattle. The lower calving intervals (377.5±34.90  day) is associated with GG genotype 
in fertile HF cattle. Moreover, higher calf birth weight 
(38.3±2  kg) is associated with GG genotype than the 
other observed genotypes in both anestrum and fertile 
animals (Table  3). Meanwhile, there are no significant 
variations in milk yield and days of milking among the 
genotypes (Table 3).
Discussion
Our hypothesis was that ovarian activity, reproductive 
and productive performance in HF cattle influence by the 
genetic variations in the NOTCH2 gene. Thus, the goal

of this study was to identify the effect of NOTCH2 gene 
polymorphisms on productive and reproductive performance in fertile and anestrum cattle. To the best of our 
knowledge, no research has been done on the relation 
between NOTCH2 gene polymorphisms and HF cattle 
reproductive and productive traits. The identification of 
four SNPs as transition single base substitution mutations located at 3: 23,192,033 (A/G), 3:23192149 (C/T), 
3:23192071 (C/T) and 3:23192143 (G/A) in Notch2 gene

of HF cattle in our study is the foremost and novel concerning their relation to the studied traits. SNPs are a 
kind of direct markers that code for functional mutation 
and regulate variation in the trait, and it is extremely very 
helpful for marker-assisted selections [22]. In human, 
mutation (NM_024408.3:c.6463G>T) in NOTCH2 gene 
was recorded to be associated with Hajdu Cheney Syndrome [23]. Furthermore, the heterozygous mutation 
p.D1853H of the NOTCH2 gene may be linked to premature ovarian insufficiency in human [24].
We found that Notch2 gene has significant effects on 
CI and birth weight regardless the fertility status. We 
observed that GG genotype is significantly lower in CI 
but higher in calf birth weight. So that, GG genotyped 
animals are the best for selection in Holstein Friesian 
cattle populations for both traits. The age at first calving 
and the interval between calvings are the reproductive 
traits most commonly employed to assess a cow’s fertility 
[6]. Because of their direct effects on the production of 
the herd, these traits are easily measured and included in 
genetic evaluations [25]. Numerous genes regulate AFC 
and CI traits, each of which has a small impact on phenotypic variation [26].
There have been no studies on NOTCH2 gene polymorphisms in cattle but more expression studies on this 
gene were conducted in animals and human. NOTCH2
may be involved in ovarian folliculogenesis because 
it is expressed in granulosa cells and oocytes during 
all phases of follicular development [12, 27, 28]. It has 
been demonstrated that NOTCH2 controls the development of primitive follicles [29]. The precise effect of the 
Notch gene SNPs on the ovarian activity of cows is still 
unknown, but Li et al. [24] reported that in women, a rare 
heterozygous NOTCH2 mutation may be linked to early 
ovarian insufficiency. In the current study, GG genotype 
is associated with calf birth weight. In this respect, a single study on NOTCH1 genes, detected five novel SNPs in

NOTCH1 gene associated with growth traits in Chinese 
cattle [30]. In our study, the GG genotype related to the 
NOTCH2 gene was positively affect reproductive traits, 
especially in fertile animals. This is due to the low calving interval, age at first calving and higher birth weights 
were observed in fertile cattle with the GG genotype. 
However, in case of anestrus animals, the GG genotype 
was also positively correlated with calving interval and 
birth weights but negatively correlated with age at first 
calving. The positively or negatively change in genotypephenotype relationship may be due to numbers and sampling status of fertile and anestrus animals. Moreover, 
our future studies on polymorphisms should involve

larger animal populations to confirm these results and

Conclusion
The investigated polymorphism in NOTCH2 gene may 
play an important role in some reproductive traits. 
The GG genotype of NOTCH2 gene may be utilize as a 
genetic marker for lower calving interval in fertile cattle 
and heavier birth weight in both fertile and anestrum 
cattle while CT genotype for higher age at first calving in 
fertile cattle. Further studies are needed to validate these 
findings across different populations with large animal 
numbers.
